 tensor([[258., 294.],
        [402., 438.]])


Now let’s look at transposed convolution, which will simply transpose \(W\):

W.T

tensor([[0., 0., 0., 0.],
        [1., 0., 0., 0.],
        [2., 1., 0., 0.],
        [0., 2., 0., 0.],
        [3., 0., 0., 0.],
        [4., 3., 1., 0.],
        [5., 4., 2., 1.],

And then multiply that by \(Y'\):

Zprime = torch.matmul(W.T, Yprime)
print("Z':\n", Zprime)
print("Z:\n", Zprime.reshape(X.shape[0], X.shape[1]))

        [ 774., 2316., 3708., 2346.],
        [2754., 6492., 7884., 4542.],
        [2412., 5442., 6282., 3504.]])


And let’s check that against the equivalent from nn:

transconv = nn.ConvTranspose2d(in_channels=1, out_channels=1,
                               kernel_size=K.shape, padding=0, 
                               stride=1, bias=False)
transconv.weight.data = K.unsqueeze(0).unsqueeze(0)
Z2 = transconv(Y.unsqueeze(0).unsqueeze(0)).squeeze(0).squeeze(0).detach()

print("Z2:\n", Z2)

Z2:
 tensor([[   0.,  258.,  810.,  588.],
        [ 774., 2316., 3708., 2346.],
        [2754., 6492., 7884., 4542.],
        [2412., 5442., 6282., 3504.]])


From the above, we can see that, just like the standard convolutional layer, the transposed convolutional layer is also defined by the padding and stride. Padding and stride are the one that hypothetically was carried out on the output to generate the input. i.e. if you take the output, and carry out a standard convolution with stride and padding defined, it will generate the spatial dimension same as that of the input.
The name “fractionally strided convolution” is used to describe the fact that the output tensor is “stretched” or “scaled up” from the input tensor, and the amount of stretching is determined by the stride of the convolutional kernel. The stride determines how much overlap there is between the kernel and the input tensor as the kernel is slid over the input tensor, and thus determines how much the output tensor is scaled up.
In practice, the “fractional” part of “fractionally strided convolution” is just a metaphor that is used to explain the concept. In actual implementation, the stride of the convolutional kernel must be an integer value, and there is no such thing as a fractional stride.
While the name “fractionally strided convolution” is not entirely accurate, it has become a standard term used in the deep learning community to refer to transposed convolutional layers that are used for upsampling or deconvolution. In practice, these layers are implemented using standard convolutional operations, but with appropriate adjustments to the kernel size, stride, and padding to achieve the desired effect.
In PyTorch, the transpose convolutional layer is implemented using torch.nn.ConvTranspose2d(). To upsample with a factor of 2, these two settings are the most common for 2D transposed convolutional layers:
nn.ConvTranspose2d(in_channels, out_channels, kernel_size=2,
                   stride=2, padding=0, dilation=1)
nn.ConvTranspose2d(in_channels, out_channels, kernel_size=4
                   stride=2, padding=1, dilation=1)
Here’s an example of those two variants, in this using a kernel of all 1s. The first example results in a non-overlapping upsample of the feature map \(Y\):

transconv2 = nn.ConvTranspose2d(in_channels=1, out_channels=1,
                                kernel_size=2, padding=0, 
                                stride=2, dilation=1, bias=False)
K3 = torch.ones(4).reshape(2, 2)
transconv2.weight.data = K3.unsqueeze(0).unsqueeze(0)
Z3 = transconv2(Y.unsqueeze(0).unsqueeze(0)).squeeze(0).squeeze(0).detach()
Z3

tensor([[258., 258., 294., 294.],
        [258., 258., 294., 294.],
        [402., 402., 438., 438.],
        [402., 402., 438., 438.]])


The second results in overlapping kernels:

transconv2 = nn.ConvTranspose2d(in_channels=1, out_channels=1,
                                kernel_size=4, padding=1,

Note



The transposed convolutional layer is also ocassionally (and incorrectly) referred to as the deconvolutional layer. A deconvolutional layer reverses the operation of a standard convolutional layer i.e. if the output generated through a standard convolutional layer is deconvolved, you get back the original input values. The transposed convolutional layer is similar to the deconvolutional layer in the sense that the spatial dimension generated by both are the same. Transposed convolution doesn’t reverse the standard convolution by values, rather by dimensions only.

3.4 Unpooling
Another approach to upsampling is unpooling, which is computationally less expensive then transposed convolutions (Khallaghi, Eastman, and Estes 2023), and is used in some encoder-decoder architectures, such as SegNet (Badrinarayanan, Kendall, and Cipolla 2017). To conceive of unpooling, let’s first revisit max pooling, which reduces the spatial resolution of the feature maps by dividing each feature map into non-overlapping regions and taking the maximum value of each region. Unpooling, on the other hand, increases the spatial resolution of the feature maps by placing the maximum value of each region to its corresponding location in the output feature map.
Let’s look at the unpooling operation in SegNet, which is performed by using tracking indices from the pooling operation in the encoder network, which record the index number of the pixel providing the max value retained after pooling. These index values are stored in “switch variables”, which are then used during the unpooling operation to place maximum values from the previous layer into the locations indicated the stored indices in the output feature, which is of the same dimensions as the pre-pooled feature map in the encoder network. The rest of the values in the output feature map are set to 0, and the unpooling layer then goes through a convolutional layer, which is used to refine the upscaled feature maps.






Figure 4: An overview of max unpooling (credit)





3.5 Encoder-decoder architectures
In the last example, where we discussed unpooling, we introduced the concept of encoder-decoder architectures, specifically referring to SegNet (Badrinarayanan, Kendall, and Cipolla 2017), so we’ll now talk a bit more about these. Encoder-decoder architectures used for semantic segmentation consists of two sub-networks: 1) an encoder network, which compresses the input image into a feature representation (i.e. the backbone), and 2) a decoder network, which produces a segmentation map by upsampling the encoded features.
We have already heard about SegNet and its unpooling operations. It’s architecture is illustrated in Figure 5. This architecture uses VGG16 as its backbone, and, similar to FCN, drops the fully-connected layers at the bottom in favor convolutional layers, and the upsampling is based on the unpooling combined with convolutional layers (not transposed convolutions). Each level of the encoder is matched by a corresponding level in the encoder, making the architecture symmetrical (unlike FCNs).






Figure 5: An overview of SegNet’s architecture (from Badrinarayanan, Kendall, and Cipolla 2017)




3.5.1 U-Net
We’ll next look at another widely used encoder-decoder architecture, U-Net (Ronneberger, Fischer, and Brox 2015), which figures heavily in Assignment 3. U-Net was originally developed for segmenting medical images, but has been broadly applied for other purposes, including for classifying satellite imagery. It’s architecture is illustrated in Figure 6. U-Net has the same symmetrical design as SegNet, and often uses a VGG variant as its backbone, typically doubling in width (number of feature maps) with each step in depth.






Figure 6: An overview of U-Net’s architectures (from Khallaghi, Eastman, and Estes 2023).



Unlike SegNet, U-Net uses transposed convolutions to upsample by a factor of 2 on each step up the encoder, halving the number of features maps in the process. The model then uses skip connections from the adjacent level of encoder to concatenate the feature maps with the same spatial resolution to the upsampled feature maps from the decoder. These concatenations are then passed through a double-convolutional layer. The last of these layers in the decoder is then passed through a softmax to make the dense prediction.
U-Nets have been modified in various ways (see Khallaghi, Eastman, and Estes 2023), particularly by replacing the encoder with alternative backbone networks, such a ResNets.



3.6 Other architectures
There are many other encoder-decoder models out there on the market, such as ExFuse (Z. Zhang et al. 2018) and Global Convolutional Networks (Peng et al. 2017), which you will learn more about by reading section 4.2 in Khallaghi, Eastman, and Estes (2023).
You should also learn about the alternative architectures that are based on pyramiding and dilated convolutions (section 4.3 in Khallaghi, Eastman, and Estes 2023), which include models such as DeepLab (Chen et al. 2019).

title: Introduction
text:
2 What is Earth Observation?
Earth Observation (EO) can be roughly defined as a combination of methods and technology used to remotely measure and monitor the patterns and processes of the Earth. EO covers a wide variety of subjects, ranging from counting individual animals to estimating crop yields to rainfall estimation to mapping land cover types (which is one of the most common applications). EO data is collected using a variety of different sensors, including multi- and hyperspectral optical, radar, and lidar, which can be mounted on orbiting satellites, aerial drones, traditional aircraft, and even kites. EO further extends to ground-based sensors streaming data via cell phone networks, street view cameras, and even to observations collected beneath the surface, using, for example, submersible vehicles to collect data from deep in the oceans.
In addition to data capture, EO involves further steps related to data processing and analysis, which can be thought of as a pipeline. First, specific techniques are used to process the captured data (e.g. to correct geometric and atmospheric distortions–you learn about this in Intro to Remote Sensing), followed by steps to convert the data into forms that can be readily analyzed. These processed images are then typically ingested by a model that is trained to extract meaning from the data. Increasingly, deep learning models are being used for this final step, given their strong capabilities to identify patterns and features of interest in various kinds of EO data.






Figure 1: Various modes of collecting Earth Observation data

title: Introduction
section: 3 A (Very) Brief History of Machine Learning in EO
text:
3 A (Very) Brief History of Machine Learning in EO
Machine learning (ML) started appearing in EO research around the late late 1990s to early 2000s, and its use has grown rapidly since. The first algorithms to be used included support vector machines (Schölkopf et al. 2000), regression trees, and Random Forests (Breiman 2001), and even early versions of artificial neural networks (ANNs). One earlier comparison of several ML algorithms for land cover mapping is provided by Rogan et al. (2008), while a more recent one is provided by Maxwell et al. (2018). Random Forests, in particular, has become a mainstay for EO applications, given its generally high performance, relative ease of implementation, and ability to achieve robust results with fairly small and even noisy training data (Elmes et al. 2020). The ease of use for Random Forests has only grown with its inclusion in Google’s Earth Engine platform (Gorelick et al. 2017), which has enabled Random Forests to be applied at increasingly large scales. Prominent examples include 30 m resolution maps of global croplands (see Xiong et al. 2017 for the approach used to map Africa’s croplands), and, more recently, a <5 m resolution map of tree cover for Southeast Asia (Yang et al. 2023).
It is interesting to note the dates of the first comparison paper (Rogan et al. 2008) and the last review paper (Maxwell et al. 2018) mentioned above, and that both papers largely cover the same ML methods, 10 years apart. This gap illustrates the lag between the availability of ML methods and their adoption by EO practitioners. Indeed, a review of land cover mapping studies conducted between 2000-2012 (cited and supported by Maxwell et al. 2018) found that nearly 1/3 of surveyed papers relied on maximum likelihood classifiers, despite the fact that machine learning classifiers were already availabile and were known to be superior (Yu et al. 2014). The authors attributed this reliance on the older, less effective classifiers to their ready availability in the image processing software typically used by EO practitioners, which at the time presumably lacked built-in machine learning classifiers.
The underlying reason for the adoption lag is because machine learning algorithms are developed in other fields, such as computer science, and are initially applied for other purposes (e.g. natural language processing). EO scientists and practitioners, who are not typically trained in machine learning techniques, had to first become familiar with these tools, then adapt them to the different modalities of EO data, and finally integrate them with their software. We can see this same lag, which appears to be about 5-10 years, in the use of deep learning models in EO. In fact, Maxwell et al. (2018) excluded deep learning from their review, stating that:

We do not consider the many new machine-learning algorithms…and deep convolution neural networks (Yue et al. 2015)], because such methods have not yet been widely adopted.

Yet breakthroughs in deep learning for image classification had been made in 2012 (Krizhevsky et al. 2012), and the widely used U-Net architecture (Ronneberger et al. 2015), first applied to segmenting cellular structures in electron microscope slides, was published three years earlier than Maxwell et al’s paper. However, things are now changing rapidly, and the use of deep learning is accelerating, such that the time lag between model availability and uptake is shrinking. One example of this shrinking is seen in the ongoing collaboration between Clark’s Center for Geospatial Analytics, NASA, and IBM, which developed a so-called foundation model (a general purpose model) for EO using a Vision Transformer model as a key compoent (Jakubik et al. 2023). The original Vision Transformer model was first published in 2021, and was originally developed for segmenting ordinary imagery (Dosovitskiy et al. 2021).
Given the emerging capabilities of deep learning models and the growing corpus of EO data, it is essential for EO professionals and data scientists interested in geospatial data to gain a working understanding of how to apply these models to derive useful insights from EO data.

title: Introduction
text:
4 Types of models and problems
There is a huge and growing variety of deep learning architectures, which fall under the general categories of convolutional neural networks, recurrent neural networks, generative adversarial networks, transformers, deep belief networks, graph neural networks, and others, with a large diversity of different types under each category, and frequent co-mingling and hybridization across these general classes (Khallaghi et al. 2023).
These models are applied to solve a variety of different problems, a number of which are listed in Dive Into Deep Learning, and includes regression problems (predicting a quantity), classification, sequence analysis, making recommendations, synthesizing data, and others. These problems can also be broken into several different kinds of sub-problems. For example, a classification problem can relate to text (e.g. the sentiment expressed a social media post) or to imagery (does the photo contain plant or an animal). For EO, the most relevant example is image classification, which can take several forms, as illustrated in Figure 2. These include segmentation segmentation, in which each pixel is grouped and assigned membership to a particular class; instance segmentation, which is when distinct groups of pixels representing individual examples (instance) of a class (e.g. a building, a tree, a crop field) are assigned individual identifiers; objection detection, where individual objects of a class or classes are detected and their locations indicated. An entire image can also be classifed; for example, the images in Figure 2 C or D could be labelled simply as “town” or “urban”.






Figure 2: Image classification problems in EO: A) multi-class and C) binary semantic segmentation; B) object detection; D) instance segmentation.



These sorts of deep learning-based classifications are often made using convolutional neural networks, which learn from spatial context. Sequence analysis, or “sequence learning” (DiDL’s phrasing) is another type of problem solved by certain classes of deep learning models, one that is highly relevant to EO. In this case, the model learns patterns that arise in sequences of data that are correlated with the relative order and distance of objects in the sequence. For example, words in a passage of text have particular relationships with one another, such as the following sentence:

Next semester, I will be attending Clark University and plan to take a class in statistics.

Each successive word narrows the scope of possible words that come after it, because speech is governed by linguistic rules that establish an order for particular kinds of words (subject noun, verb, adjective, object noun), and certain words are used more often with some words and less often with others. By the time you get to the end of the sentence above, class in would be most plausibly associated with a word or phrase that is associated with classes offered at a University. There are deep learning models that learn the relationships between words in passages of text so that they can predict what words are most likely to come next.
In EO, satellite image time series are image sequences that capture temporal changes on the Earth’s surface arising from seasonality, weather, or disturbances. The relative order and magnitude of these changes, encoded in reflectance (or radar backscatter), varies according to the nature of the surface feature and process. For example, a time series of Sentinel-2 images collected over the course of a year will produce an NDVI curve that looks very different over a forest than one collected over buildings (Figure 3).








Figure 3: A time series of NDVI from Sentinel-2 imagery collectd over a farm in northeastern South Africa. One point was collected over a tree plantation, the other over a group of farm buildings.





These temporal sequences can be learned and associated with different land cover types, so that those types can be predicted. We used this approach in a recent project to map crop types in Ghana and Tanzania, using time series of both Sentinel-1 and 2 along with a 1-D convolutional neural network to map maize and rice (Wussah et al. 2022).
In this course, we will focus primarily on solving EO classification problems, particularly semantic segmentation, using convolutional networks. We will also learn about models that can learn from satellite time series to solve classification problems. In addition to these, we will touch on generative models and their role in both synthesizing and classifying imagery, and cover attention mechanisms, the building blocks of transformers, which are rapidly growing in use (see Section 3).
That was a very brief overview of what we’ll cover in this course. We’ll now turn next to learning some of the basics of neural networks.

title: Foreword
text:
This course covers the intersection of two large and rapidly expanding fields, Earth Observation (EO, or remote sensing) and deep learning (DL), which is key to the rapidly burgeoning field of artificial intelligence (AI). You will also see that the term GeoAI, or geospatial artificial intelligence, is increasingly used, and encompasses this convergence. title: Convolutional neural networks
text:
So far we have learned a bit about multi-layer perceptrons, a type of neural network that is characterized by the fact that it is fully connected (each node in one layer is connected to every node in the subsequent layer). This complete connectedness enables the model to learn complex functions, but it has some disadvantages also. One disadvantage is that the number of parameters can get very large in networks with many nodes and multiple hidden layers (you answer a question related to this in assignment 1, in fact). The second is that they have difficulties detecting features if they appear in a different location, or at a different scale, in the input dataset. That is because there is a separate weight learned for each individual input node, and weights are not shared across nodes, an MLP can only learn patterns based on where they appear in the data that were used to train the model. In other words, the patterns learned depend on the locations where they are found in the input data.
To illustrate this last point, we will use the example of handwritten digits in the MNIST dataset that we will train an MLP to recognize in our first assignment. In Figure 1, we see one example of a handwritten 4 from training dataset. The top four panels show the image after torchvision.transforms.RandomCrop() was applied to it, shifting the digits slightly (by up to 4 pixels in any direction). That transformation introduced a bit of spatial variation into the training sample, enabling the model to learn patterns that occurred in slightly different positions. However, what would happen if you wanted to train a model that could identify digits in a much larger input image, regardless of where they appear in the image? If the scale of the digits remained the same, and the images were 4X larger, as in panels E-F, there are many more places each digit could appear. For the model to learn to recognize those patterns anywhere, a much larger sample would be needed to account for that, and many more parameters would have to be calculated–recall, each pixel in the image is an input node, so an image that is 56X56 has 3,136 nodes, and if connects to a hidden layer with 1000 nodes, that is 3,137,000 learnable parameters, compared to 785,000 parameters for the 28X28 input image.






Figure 1: Examples of one of the training images from the MNIST data. Panels A-D show the original data and three randomly cropped permutations, where the image was randomly cropped within a 32X32 canvas to size 28X28, resulting in a shift of up to 4 pixels in one or both of the X and Y dimension. Panels E-F show the same digit within a canvas nearly 4 times larger.



The problem becomes even harder if you want the model to be able to recognize digits anywhere they appear in the image, regardless of their scale, i.e. you also want to be to distinguish 4s from other numbers regardless of whether they are very large or very small. You would need to increase your training sample even more.
The issue here is that we want the model to be able to recognize patterns, regardless of where and what scale they appear in the input data. This ability is related to the concept of invariance (or equivariance), which holds that the model’s capabilities should be invariant to where values of interest are found in the input. Convolutional neural networks (CNNs) are designed to provide this capability, which they achieve by processing the information at multiple scales, starting by finding relationships among immediately neighboring input values (the , and then progressively aggregating these in deep layers of the network to learn patterns across larger scales.






Note 1: Locality



To achieve invariance, CNNs leverage the principle of locality, which holds that objects close to one another are likely to be correlated, whereas those farther apart are likely to be less correlated. This is a fairly basic idea in geography, and also is in physics, where it is stated that “that an object is influenced directly only by its immediate surroundings” (Wikipedia). In CNNs, the first layers focus on learning patterns in small areas, and the size of the areas examined become progressively larger with each successive layer (DiDL).


CNNs, which were initially designed to work with images, achieve invariance by using layers consisting of convolutions, or sliding windows (similar to what we have used in remote sensing for many years when we apply texture measures to imagery, e.g. Estes et al. 2008; Tuceryan and Jain 1993; Wulder et al. 1998) to convert each pixel in an image into a function of the values extracted from the pixels in a small neighborhood immediately around it (e.g. 3X3, 5X5). This use of convolutions gives CNNs an inductive bias (that is, the a set of assumptions that shapes what sort of patterns they can learn) towards detecting objects in images, and it also enables them to have vastly fewer parameters than MLPs.

title: Convolutional neural networks
text:
2 What are CNNs?
As described above, CNNs are a kind of neural network that is specialized for processing structured data that have a grid-like topology. They use convolutions in place of general matrix multiplication, in at least one of their layers. The design of a CNN is inspired by the visual cortex in the brain, which contains a larger number of cells that function by detecting light in small, overlapping sub-regions of the visual field, which are called receptive fields. These cells act as local filters over the input space, and the more complex cells have larger receptive fields. The convolution layer in a CNN performs the function that is performed by the cells in the visual cortex.






Convolutions and other forms of data



Although we will primarily examine CNNs that work with images, convolutional layers can process other types of structured inputs that are important in EO, such as 1d temporal, 3d spatio-temporal, or 3d spatio-spectral structures. They can even be used to recognize 4D spatio-temporal-spectral patterns.

title: Convolutional neural networks
text:
3 CNN components
A basic CNN usually consists of a varying combinations of the following layers:

Convolutional layers (e.g. conv1d, conv2d, conv3d)
Activation function layer (e.g. ReLU)
Normalization (e.g. batch normalization)
Sub-sampling layers (e.g. some type of pooling layer)
Fully connected layers
Classifier (e.g. sigmoid, softmax)

We have already discussed activation functions when we learned about MLPs and basic neural networks, so we won’t return to those here (but will note here that ReLu is widely used in CNNs). In addition to that, since batch normalization is an important component of many neural networks, and we have already asked you to include batch normalization in your first assignment, we won’t go into that here. However, we will come back to that later, so in preparation please read section 2.3 in (Khallaghi, Eastman, and Estes 2023), and the relevant section in Dive Into Deep Learning.
We will now look at the remaining components in more detail.

3.1 2D convolutions
We can think of 2d convolution as template matching, since the output at a point (i,j) will be large if the corresponding image patch centered on (i,j) is similar to W. If the template W corresponds to an oriented edge, then convolving with it will cause the output heat map to “light up” in regions that contain edges that match that orientation. More generally, we can think of convolution as a form of feature detection. The resulting output Y = W * X is therefore called a feature map.
A convolution layer in a CNN imposes a number of restrictions compared to a more general fully connected layer. For one, the connections in the network are confined to a limited spatial neighborhood that is determined by the kernel size. The result is that not every node in layer L is connected to every node in layer L+1, which stands in contrast to fully connected neural networks, where every node is connected to every other in the following layer. This means that if we limit the number of connections for each input to k we need k x n parameters and O(k×n) runtime. In a fully connected network, with m inputs and n outputs in a linear layer, matrix multiplication requires m x n parameters and O(m×n) runtime per example. k is typically much smaller than m.
Second, weights are shared, which means that the same weights are applied to all receptive fields in a layer. In a CNN, since the kernels are smaller than the input (k << m), each filter is applied to every position in the input, i.e., same filter is used for all local receptive fields (neighborhoods). As the filter moves around the image, the same weights are applied to each f x f set of nodes. Each filter, as such, can be trained to perform a certain specific transformation of the input space. Therefore, each filter has a certain set of weights that are applied for each convolution operation – this greatly reduces the number of trainable parameters. Less parameters results in an easier optimization problem, without losing much generality.
Multiple convolution filters are usually learned in every layer, which act as a set of spatial feature detectors. Further, convolutions preserve information about the location of input features (modulo reduced resolution), providing the property known as invariance, or equivariance.
In PyTorch, convolutional layers are implemented through nn.ConvXd, where X is replaced by the proper dimensions (1,2, or 3). Since we are talking here about 2D convolutions, it would be nn.Conv2d.

3.1.1 2D Convolution operation
A convolution is calculated by summing the element-wise multiplication of pixel values in an input patch (neighborhood) by the corresponding values in the kernel’s weight matrix (Figure 2).






Figure 2: 2D convolution operation on a grey-scale input (credit)



We can extend the definition of convolution to multispectral input (e.g. 2d conv over 3d input) by defining a kernel for each input channel; thus now W is a 3d weight matrix or tensor.






Convolution versus cross-correlation



While we use the term convolution here (as is more generally done in deep learning), the actual operation is technically a cross-correlation. Convolution entails flipping the kernel, whereas the kernel is not flipped in cross-correlation. For more details for DiDL.


We compute the output by cross-correlating channel c of the input with kernel W[:,:,c], and then sum over channels (Figure 3). Each filter has one kernel per input channel (3 in this example), which are summed once run to make a single output feature map, which becomes one in the specified number of features maps (2 in this example). In the next layer, each filter will have two kernels, one per feature map in the input.






Figure 3: 2D convolution operation on a 3-band multispectral input (credit)



Each filter tries to identify a particular type of spatial pattern in a small rectangular region of the image (receptor field), and thus many filters are needed to capture the variety of possible shapes in the image. These shapes are combined in later layers, where they are used to recognize more complex patterns and eventually produce the output prediction.






Convolutional filters, shapes, and network depth



The activations of the filters in the early layers are low-level features like edges, whereas those in later layers put together these low-level features. For example, a mid-level feature might put together edges to create a hexagon, whereas a higher-level feature might put together the mid-level hexagons to create a honeycomb.


The number of filters used in each layer controls the capacity of the model because it directly controls the number of parameters.
We are talking here about 2D-convolution, but 3D-convolution is also practiced. In 2D convolution over a volume, the depth of a filter is always the same as that of the layer to which it is applied to (e.g. the three inputs bands). In a 3D convolution, the convolution layer also moves in the 3D-dimension, with some specified width that may be less than the total volume (Figure 4).






Figure 4: a) 2D convolution over a multispectral input(volume) versus b) 3D convolution (credit)





3.1.2 Padding
Since 2D convolutions are moving windows that cover a neighborhood larger than 1 pixel, they always have the problem of dealing with pixels on or near the edge. This poses two problems:

Edge pixels contribute less in the output of the convolution.
Without adjustments, the output size is reduced by the half-width of the kernel

Padding, which often takes the form of adding one or more zeros to the image border, addresses these two problems, by allowing us to keep more information at the border of an image. Adding padding is often referred to as same convolution. Without padding, very few values at the next layer would be affected by pixels at the edges of an image. It also allows you to use a convolutional layer without necessarily shrinking the height and width of the volumes. This is important for building deeper networks, since otherwise the height/width can shrink to nothing if the network is deep enough. Another issue is more technical: coding with same convolutions is easier, and the modeling pipeline can become more flexible regarding the size of the input.






Note 2: Padding terminology




Valid convolution: Convolutions without padding
Same convolution: Padding added to make the output size equal to the input size.
Full convolution: In this setting every possible partial or complete superimposition of the kernel on the input feature map is taken into account. Full padding convolution starts by matching the right corner of the kernel to the lower left corner of the corresponding image patch, and continues until the upper right corner of the kernel matches the lower left corner of the image patch, resulting in an output with a bigger size than the original input.





3.1.3 Stride
Stride is the number of pixels by which we shift our kernel over the input matrix each time it is moved. Since each output pixel is generated by a weighted combination of inputs in its receptive field (based on the size of the filter), neighoring outputs will be very similar in value, since their inputs are overlapping. We can reduce this redundancy (and speedup computation) by skipping every \(s^{th}\) input. This is called strided convolution.
When the stride is 1 then we move the filters one pixel at a time. When the stride is 2, then the filters jump 2 pixels at a time as we slide them around.
A conv layer with stride of 2 downscales the output by factor of 2. For this reason a conv layer with a stride > 1 can be used to downsample the image.






What is a receptive field?



The size (height and width) of the filter defines its receptive field (RF), or the set of pixels on which a neuron depends. It quantifies how far a neuron can “see” in the image. Note that the size of the filter can be modified in each layer.
In most applications, a large amount of spatial context must be taken into account in order to successfully label the images. For example, to determine that a certain pixel belongs to a rooftop, it is likely insufficient to just consider its individual spectrum: we will need to observe the area around this pixel, taking into account the geometry and structure of the objects, to infer its correct class.
The effective receptive field (ERF) refers to the area of the original image that can influence the activation of a neuron in an intermediate hidden layer. Whereas the RF is simply equal to the filter size in the previous layer, the ERF tracks back through each layer back to the input image, and indicates the extent of the input image that affects the activity of the neuron in the given intermediate layer. The RF and ERF are the same for the first convolutional layer. The RF in deeper layers is larger than the RF of units in shallow layers.



The effective receptive field (credit)


Calculating the size of the ERF helps a CNN developer to choose suitable filter sizes for addressing particular tasks. From a Geographer’s perspective, the ERF can be tied to the characteristic scale of the objects of interest in the landscape being analyzed.
Examining the RF and convolution operations shows that not all pixels in a receptive field contribute equally to an output unit’s response. Pixels at the center of a receptive field have a much larger impact on an output. In the forward pass of the model, central pixels can provide information to the output through many different paths, while the pixels in the outer area of the RF have few paths to propagate their impact. In the backward pass, gradients from an output unit are propagated across all the paths, and therefore the central pixels have a much larger magnitude in the gradient from that output.
Further studies showed in many cases, the distribution of impact in an RF has a Gaussian distribution. This implies that the effective area in the RF only occupies a fraction of the theoretical RF, as Gaussian distributions generally decay quickly from the center.
The Gaussian effect is most pronounced when using valid convolutions, less influential with same (padded) convolutions, and mostly disappears with full convolution.





3.2 1×1 (pointwise) convolution
Sometimes we just want to take a weighted combination of the features at a given location, rather than across locations. This can be done using 1x1 convolutions, also called pointwise convolution. This changes the number of channels from \(C\) to \(D\), without changing spatial dimensions. Pointwise convolution can be conceived of as a single layer MLP applied through each column of a stack of feature maps.
1X1 convolutions can be used to either reduce or expand dimensionality, but are most typically used for the former purpose. They are widely used in many modern architectures, such as the Inception module in GoogLeNet, in order to reduce the number of parameters and computational cost.






Figure 5: Conceptual figure showing the use of 1X1 convolution to reduce a set of 192 features maps to 1, while retaining the 64X64 spatial dimensions (credit)





3.3 Pooling layers
A pooling layer operates on blocks of the input feature map to spatially aggregate the feature activations. This aggregation operation is commonly defined by a fixed function, such as the average or the max functions, and has no learnable parameters in the backpropagation step.
The purpose of the pooling layer is twofold:

To further increase spatial invariance by reducing the resolution of the feature maps, without increasing the number of learnable parameters in the network.
To increase the receptive field throughout the network.

The use of pooling can be thought of as adding an assumption that the function the layer learns must be invariant to small translations. When this assumption is correct, it can greatly improve the statistical eﬃciency of the network. Setting the size of the pooling kernel decides how invariant or robust to distortions we want the representation to be. It is best to pool slowly throughout the network after a few convolution layers.
The size of the output of the pooling layer depends on the stride between the pools, the pool kernel size, and spatial dimensions of its the input.
\[
\begin{align}
h' & = \lfloor\frac{h-f+s}{s}\rfloor\\  
w' & = \lfloor\frac{w-f+s}{s}\rfloor \\
\end{align}
\]
The computational cost of the pooling layer is proportional to the size of the input, and is negligible compared to a convolutional layer. Usually we choose a pooling stride that gives us non-overlapping regions, and zero-padding is often used in pooling operations. Pooling is separately applied to each feature map.
The most common pooling technique is max-pooling. Max-pooling simply outputs the maximum value in the input region. An alternative is to use average pooling, which replaces the max by the mean. In either case, the output neuron has the same response no matter where the input pattern occurs within its receptive field.










Figure 6: Max (left) and average (right) pooling of a 4X4 input using a 2X2 kernel (credit)



Max pooling provides significant help in pattern recognition, because it discards less significant data while preserving the detected features in a smaller representation. The reasoning behind pooling operations is that feature detection is more important than the feature’s exact location. Computing the maximum value is inspired by the idea of detecting objects from their parts. For example, in a face detector it is important to identify the constituents of a face, such as hair or nose, while the exact locations of these components should not be a determinant factor. The max pooling layer conveys then to which extent there is evidence of the existence of a particular feature in a given vicinity.
The downside of pooling operations (and downsampling in general) is that it hard-codes robustness to spatial deformations, a virtue that boosted the success of CNNs for simple problems, such as image categorization. However, spatial precision is lost when downsampling. The increased RF (and thus recognition capability) comes at the price of losing localization capability. This well-reported trade-off is a major concern for dense prediction problems (e.g. semantic segmentation).
Max and average pooling are implemented as nn.MaxPoolXd and nn.AvgPoolXd, respectively, in PyTorch.

3.3.1 Pooling variants
If we average over all the locations in a feature map, the method is called global average pooling, which enables us to convert a H × W × D feature map into a 1 × 1 × D dimensional feature map. This can be further reshaped to a D-dimensional vector and passed into a fully connected (FC) layer, then mapped to a C-dimensional vector before passing into a softmax output. The use of global average pooling means we can apply the classifier to an image of any size, since the final feature map will always be converted to a fixed D-dimensional vector before being mapped to a distribution over the C classes. Alternatively, we can use global max pooling.
This layer is implemented under the name nn.AdaptiveMaxPoolXd and nn.AdaptiveAvgPoolXd.

title: Convolutional neural networks
text:
4 A complete CNN
An example of a simple CNN archiecture with two convolutional layers wth ReLu activations, followed by pooling and a final classifier, is shown in Figure 7, where a 3-band RGB image is fed into a network that starts with a convolutional layer with 10 filters with a 3x3 kernel and ReLu activation, followed by a pooling that reduces the spatial dimensions by a factor of 2, followed by a second convolutional layer with 20 filters, which is again pooled and then passed through two fully connected layers to a final classification into one of four values.






Figure 7: An example of a simple CNN architecture with two convolutional layers, two poolings, and two fully connected layers leading to a 4-class prediction.



A more complex CNN is illustrated in Figure 8, which is the structure of VGG-16 (Simonyan and Zisserman 2015), a model designed to classify imagery from the ImageNet benchmark dataset into one of a thousand classes. The model takes an input image with 3 bands and spatial dimensions of 224x224, and consists of several layers in which pairs or triplets of convolutional layers with kernel sizes of 3x3 followed by ReLu activations that are fed to a max pooling layer, which reduces the output dimensions by a factor of 2. The number of filters in the convolutional layer are doubled in each successive layer.






Figure 8: An example of a more complex CNN architecture, in this case VGG-16 (credit).



For example, the first level has two convolutional layers, each with 64 filters, and each followed by a ReLu activation, resulting in feature maps of 224x224, which are then pooled to 112x112. These are then fed to the next two convolutional layers, each of which have 128 filters. The final set of convolutional layers have three separate sets of convolutional layers each having 512 filters with dimensions of 14x14, which are then pooled to 7x7 and passed to 3 fully connected (FC) layers (i.e. an MLP), followed by a softmax classifier. To go into the FCs, the output of the final max pooled layer is flattened from 7x7x512 to 1x1x2058, and then enters the first FC of 1x1x4096, followed by a second of the same size, and a third of 1X1X1000 (matching the number of predicted classes).






Sequential convolutional layers



Stacking two convolutional layers, each with 3X3 kernels, produces a RF that is equivalent to that of a single convolutional layer with a 5X5 kernel size, but for fewer learnable parameters (Khallaghi, Eastman, and Estes 2023).
Note that a layer with a single convolutional filter with a kernel size of 3x3 receiving a 3 band input image will have 3x3x3 weights plus a bias, resulting in 28 learnable parameters. The same layer with a 5x5 kernel will have 5x5x3+1 (76) learnable parameters, thus stacking two layers, each with a single 3x3 kernel filter will require only 54 parameters, which is 71% of the parameters of the layer with a single 5x5 kernal filter.

title: Multi-layer perceptrons
text:
In the previous chapter we learned about the basics of neural networks, and discussed briefly a particular type of neural network, the multi-layer percepton. In this chapter, we are going to learn more about this particular model, while getting some more details on the ingredients and how to run neural networks.
As described in the previous chapter, a multilayer perceptron (MLP) (read linked content) is a feedforward fully connected neural network. It is feedforward, because, as we have already heard, the computation passes the input values toward the output in a forward direction creating an acyclic graph (e.g. with no cycles or backward links). It is fully-connected because each node after the input layer receives input from every node in the previous layer, making the dense connectivity (e.g. full pairwise connection) shown in Figure 1 below. The hierarchical structure of the network implies that the graphics represent a nested function.
An MLP usually consists of 3 or more layers: an input layer, an output layer and one or more hidden layers also called dense or FC layers. We know the values of the nodes in the first layer (e.g. our input), and the number of output neurons will be equal to the number of classes in the classification problem. All others are hidden neurons, and the layers that contain them are called hidden layers.
Sections 5.2 and 5.3 (read these) in Dive into Deep Learning explains the implementation of MLP and inner workings of computational graphs and relevent algorithms.






Figure 1: Example architecture of a MLP with two hidden layers and a single output node (credit)









Note



As discussed in the last chapter, we generally call a neural net with a single hidden layer a shallow neural network, and refer to a network with two or more hidden layers as a deep neural network. However, this terminology is not universal, and sometimes you will see the words “shallow” and “deep” used subjectively to denote networks with a “few” and with “many” layers, respectively.
Beside having more hidden layers, modern deep neural networks have other improvements, such as better activation functions (e.g. ReLU family), and usually include batch normalization and dropout layers in their design.


We described previously how each computation unit in a FC layer accepts the input, multiplies weights, adds the bias, and applies an activation function to it before forwarding it to the next layer. This activated output becomes input for the computation units in the next layer.
Refreshing ourselves on the formulas seen before (but presenting them slightly differently), each unit in a dense layer therefore performs the computations as shown below, the first of which involves an affine transformation of the input, while the second computation is to apply a point-wise non-linearity to the output of the first stage.
\[
\begin{align}
a_1 &= W_1 I + b_1 \\
z_1 &= \sigma_1(a_1)
\end{align}
\tag{1}\]
Where \(\sigma_1\) is the non-linear function in the first layer, \(W_1\) is the weight matrix represented by the connections between the input layer \(I\) (with 6 features, or nodes) in Figure 1, and \(b_0\) is the bias vector. Note that Equation 1 is a two-stage equivalent of Equation 6 in the previous chapter.
For the next layer (e.g. in our example its the second hidden layer), the calculation is as follows:
\[
\begin{align}
a_2 &= W_2 z_1 + b_2 \\
z_2 &= \sigma_2(a_2)
\end{align}
\]
A third pair of these equations would connect the second layer and the output. A general form of the these can be written as:
\[
z_l = \sigma_l(z_{l-1}) = \sigma_l(b_l + W_l(z_{l-1}))\\
\]

2 Commonly used activation functions
Up to now, we have mentioned activation functions, and the fact that they introduce non-linearity into the networks, but haven’t really given any detail, so we will look at a few of the more widely used ones (and you should familiarize yourself with the relevant section (read this) in Dive into Deep Learning.
The activation function in a neural network has a huge impact on the model’s final performance, thus the choice of activation function used in the network is crucial.
We’ll first show two exponentiated functions, sigmoid and tanh, which were among the first used (and are still used in certain kinds of networks), but are now largely replaced by the simpler and less computationally intensive ReLu (and its derivatives). The reason for their replacement is many deep neural networks that use these two functions, and which are trained using backpropagation, suffer from the problem of vanishing gradients (read this).

2.1 Sigmoid (logistic) function
The sigmoid, or logistic, function (Figure 2) was one of the first used in neural networks. It maps real numbers into the unit interval (0, 1), which is useful if you want to transform a real-valued variable into something that represents a probability. This function is used as an activation, and also can be used at the end of the network in order to classify binary variables (for multi-class mappings, softmax is used).








Figure 2: The sigmoid function and its derivative.







2.2 Hyperbolic tangent
The hyperbolic tangent, or tanh is sometimes called the bipolar sigmoidal function. It maps real numbers into the interval (−1, 1), having horizontal asymptotes at \(y = ±1\).
The advantage of tanh over sigmoid is that the negative inputs will be mapped strongly negative and the zero inputs will be mapped near zero in the tanh graph, and the graph of tanh(x) is symmetric with respect to the origin.








Figure 3: The tanh function and its derivative.







2.3 Rectified Linear Unit (ReLU)
A rectified linear unit (ReLu) is easy to optimize because it is very close to linear. The only difference between a linear unit and a ReLu is that the latter outputs zero across half of its domain.








Figure 4: The ReLu function and its derivative.

2 Attention
Attention mechanisms are a particular structure in neural networks that are designed to highlight the most essential features to focus on in the inputs, and to de-emphasize the least important information. These structures have become increasingly important as they are the building blocks of transformers (Vaswani et al., n.d.), which underpin many of the most recent breakthroughs in AI capabilities associated with large language models (LLMs), and more recently for vision-based tasks (Dosovitskiy et al. 2021). They are also used to enhance the capabilities of other neural network architectures, including CNNs. Attention mechanisms are covered in section 6 of part 2 of Khallaghi et al. (2025) , as well as a dedicated chapter in Dive Into Deep Learning, and there are a number of good blog posts that cover these. Please read these to learn more about the mechanisms and how they are used. Here we will give a brief summary of attention mechanisms, with a focus on how these connect to CNNs designed for semantic segmentation.

2.1 Attention mechanisms
Attention comes in two forms–hard and soft–with the former being deterministic, and the latter probabilistic and able to be differentiated, which means it can be readily incorporated into models that use backpropagation. An attention mechanism typically has a triplet structure of query (Q), key (K), and value (V), which can be best understood thinking in terms of a relational database (as explained in DiDL). In this analogy, a database consists of a set of keys (K), with each having a corresponding value (V). The database can then be searched with a query (Q) that matches a particular set of keys, so that the associated values can be received. The most important concept to understand is that the matching is done using some function that calculates a set of weights that applies across all keys that indicates the strength of the match between Q and each key. In a database, the weight corresponding to an exact match will equal 1.
This is the general concept for attention in neural networks, but it’s a little different. the query is a transformation of the input that represents the current piece to focus on, the key is the other elements on the input to compare the query against in order to find the greatest similarities with the key, which provides attention weights, which are then used to transform the values of the original input.

def rotate_image_and_label(image, label, angle):
    """
    Applies rotation augmentation to an image patch and label.

    Args:
        image (numpy array) : The input image patch as a numpy array.
        label (numpy array) : The corresponding label as a numpy array.
        angle (lost of floats) : If the list has exactly two elements they will
            be considered the lower and upper bounds for the rotation angle
            (in degrees) respectively. If number of elements are bigger than 2,
            then one value is chosen randomly as the roatation angle.

    Returns:
        A tuple containing the rotated image patch and label as numpy arrays.
    """
    if isinstance(angle, tuple) or isinstance(angle, list):
        if len(angle) == 2:
            rotation_degree = random.uniform(angle[0], angle[1])
        elif len(angle) > 2:
            rotation_degree = random.choice(angle)
        else:
            raise ValueError("Parameter degree needs at least two elements.")
    else:
        raise ValueError(
            "Rotation bound param for augmentation must be a tuple or list."
        )

    # Define the center of the image patch
    center = tuple(np.array(label.shape)/2.0)

    # Define the rotation matrix
    rotation_matrix = cv2.getRotationMatrix2D(center, rotation_degree, 1.0)

    # Apply rotation augmentation to the image patch
    rotated_image = cv2.warpAffine(image, rotation_matrix, image.shape[:2],
                                   flags=cv2.INTER_LINEAR)

    # Apply rotation augmentation to the label
    rotated_label = cv2.warpAffine(label, rotation_matrix, label.shape[:2],
                                   flags=cv2.INTER_NEAREST)

    # Return the rotated image patch and label as a tuple
    return rotated_image.copy(), np.rint(rotated_label.copy())


#@title Image flipping (`cv2`)
def flip_image_and_label(image, label, flip_type):
    """
    Applies horizontal or vertical flip augmentation to an image patch and label

    Args:
        image (numpy array) : The input image patch as a numpy array.
        label (numpy array) : The corresponding label as a numpy array.
        flip_type (string) : Based on the direction of flip. Can be either
            'hflip' or 'vflip'.

    Returns:
        A tuple containing the flipped image patch and label as numpy arrays.
    """
    if flip_type == 'hflip':
        # Apply horizontal flip augmentation to the image patch
        flipped_image = cv2.flip(image, 1)

        # Apply horizontal flip augmentation to the label
        flipped_label = cv2.flip(label, 1)

    elif flip_type == 'vflip':
        # Apply vertical flip augmentation to the image patch
        flipped_image = cv2.flip(image, 0)

        # Apply vertical flip augmentation to the label
        flipped_label = cv2.flip(label, 0)

    else:
        raise ValueError("Flip direction must be 'horizontal' or 'vertical'.")

    # Return the flipped image patch and label as a tuple
    return flipped_image.copy(), flipped_label.copy()


class Evaluator(object):
    def __init__(self, num_class):
        self.num_class = num_class
        self.confusion_matrix = np.zeros((self.num_class,)*2)

    def Pixel_Accuracy(self):
        # Overall Pixel Accuracy
        Acc = np.diag(self.confusion_matrix).sum() / self.confusion_matrix.sum()
        return Acc

    def Mean_Intersection_over_Union(self):
        # Mean IoU
        MIoU = np.diag(self.confusion_matrix) / (
            np.sum(self.confusion_matrix, axis=1) +
            np.sum(self.confusion_matrix, axis=0) -
            np.diag(self.confusion_matrix)
        )
        MIoU = np.nanmean(MIoU)
        return MIoU

    def _generate_matrix(self, gt_image, pre_image):
        mask = (gt_image >= 0) & (gt_image < self.num_class)
        label = self.num_class * gt_image[mask].astype('int') + pre_image[mask]
        count = np.bincount(label, minlength=self.num_class**2)
        confusion_matrix = count.reshape(self.num_class, self.num_class)
        return confusion_matrix

    def add_batch(self, gt_image, pre_image):
        assert gt_image.shape == pre_image.shape
        self.confusion_matrix += self._generate_matrix(gt_image, pre_image)

    def reset(self):
        self.confusion_matrix = np.zeros((self.num_class,) * 2)

#@title Rotation transformation (`cv2`)
def rotate_image_and_label(image, label, angle):
    """
    Applies rotation augmentation to an image patch and label.

    Args:
        image (numpy array) : The input image patch as a numpy array.
        label (numpy array) : The corresponding label as a numpy array.
        angle (lost of floats) : If the list has exactly two elements they will
            be considered the lower and upper bounds for the rotation angle
            (in degrees) respectively. If number of elements are bigger than 2,
            then one value is chosen randomly as the roatation angle.

    Returns:
        A tuple containing the rotated image patch and label as numpy arrays.
    """
    if isinstance(angle, tuple) or isinstance(angle, list):
        if len(angle) == 2:
            rotation_degree = random.uniform(angle[0], angle[1])
        elif len(angle) > 2:
            rotation_degree = random.choice(angle)
        else:
            raise ValueError("Parameter degree needs at least two elements.")
    else:
        raise ValueError(
            "Rotation bound param for augmentation must be a tuple or list."
        )

    # Define the center of the image patch
    center = tuple(np.array(label.shape)/2.0)

    # Define the rotation matrix
    rotation_matrix = cv2.getRotationMatrix2D(center, rotation_degree, 1.0)

    # Apply rotation augmentation to the image patch
    rotated_image = cv2.warpAffine(image, rotation_matrix, image.shape[:2],
                                   flags=cv2.INTER_LINEAR)

    # Apply rotation augmentation to the label
    rotated_label = cv2.warpAffine(label, rotation_matrix, label.shape[:2],
                                   flags=cv2.INTER_NEAREST)

    # Return the rotated image patch and label as a tuple
    return rotated_image.copy(), np.rint(rotated_label.copy())

def flip_image_and_label(image, label, flip_type):
    """
    Applies horizontal or vertical flip augmentation to an image patch and label

    Args:
        image (numpy array) : The input image patch as a numpy array.
        label (numpy array) : The corresponding label as a numpy array.
        flip_type (string) : Based on the direction of flip. Can be either
            'hflip' or 'vflip'.

    Returns:
        A tuple containing the flipped image patch and label as numpy arrays.
    """
    if flip_type == 'hflip':
        # Apply horizontal flip augmentation to the image patch
        flipped_image = cv2.flip(image, 1)

        # Apply horizontal flip augmentation to the label
        flipped_label = cv2.flip(label, 1)

    elif flip_type == 'vflip':
        # Apply vertical flip augmentation to the image patch
        flipped_image = cv2.flip(image, 0)

        # Apply vertical flip augmentation to the label
        flipped_label = cv2.flip(label, 0)

    else:
        raise ValueError("Flip direction must be 'horizontal' or 'vertical'.")

    # Return the flipped image patch and label as a tuple
    return flipped_image.copy(), flipped_label.copy()

title: Final Projects
text: The following is an overview of expectations for delivering the final project.

title: Final Projects
text:
Set-up
Work with your team to set up a single private repo on the agroimpacts GitHub organization or one of your personal profiles. One of you can set it up, and then add the rest of you as contributors. Name the repo so that it describes the project, and is all in lowercase with no underscores. Short is better.

title: Final Projects
text:
Key components

Project description
Make a folder in your repo called “notebooks”, and within save a single colab notebook named description.ipynb. The notebook should contain the following sections.

Summary: A brief (up to 250 words) description of the project and its objectives (10 points).
Division of labor: A description of who did what on the project (5 points).
Key findings: A very short summary of key findings (5 points).

Commit the notebook in the repo when you are done with it in colab. You may also wish to do this locally in jupyter notebook/jupyter lab. This notebook is basically an abstract.


Primary analyses
Your final project is built in the same repository, following the steps outlined in description.iypnb.
Each sub-team in the final project group should have a notebook that lays out the analysis undertaken by the sub-team. For example, in the drone image labeling project, the team developing the cranberry models could have a notebook called prithvi-finetuning-smallsample.ipynb, and the group working on cropland mapping with the Lacuna Fund labels could have a notebook called resunet-train-mostaccurate.ipynb.
Final notebooks should have the following structure:

Introduction: A brief summary of your sub-team’s project objectives (<250 words).
Methods: A summary of the approach used to attain the objectives. E.g. what data you use, how did you process it, what model did you use, and how did you adapt it. This section should be brief but informative. Provide references to code used, etc.
Results/analysis: A brief description of the results, interleaved with any analytical steps. For instance, show:

Your model training/fine-tuning loop.
You evaluation metrics
Prediction code and predictions results (tiles/chips resulting from the prediction step)

Discussion: A brief summary of main findings, any difficulties or surprises encountered, and what improvements could be made.

Each sub-team/contributor should have a notebook that aligns with this structure. If there is a compelling reason to have a different structure, please let us know and we can come to an arrangement.
Note, mark clearly who authored the notebook. If two people are working on the same notebook, please place initials for who did what on that notebook.


Repo and code organization
It is acceptable to have all code needed to undertake the sub-team/team project in the relevant notebook, including model code, etc. In this case, we would expect to see the repo organized as reponame with one sub-folder named notebooks, with the required notebooks (including the original .ipynb) in the folder. The structure will look something like this:
.
└── reponame/
    ├── README.md
    └── notebooks/
        ├── description.ipynb
        ├── subteam-1.ipynb (named descriptively)
        └── subteam-2.ipynb (named descriptively)
The README should have the project name/brief description of the project, the names of the contributors, and a link to description.ipynb.
It may also be preferable for large blocks of reusable code to go into .py files that are loaded as modules from your repo. In this case, the structure would like more like this:
.
└── reponame/
    ├── README.md
    ├── notebooks/
    │   ├── plan.ipynb
    │   ├── subteam-1.ipynb (named descriptively)
    │   └── subteam-2.ipynb (named descriptively)
    └── reponame/
        ├── __init__.py
        ├── code1.py (e.g. unet.py)
        └── code2.py (e.g. dataloader.py)
For example, the model architecture, data loader, etc, can all go into a sub-folder in your repo named the same as the repo main folder (note: see the naming convention for the repo above). If you have an __init__.py file in the folder, then the modules can be imported into your notebooks and used there. In colab, you can clone and read in your repository by placing code such as the following in our notebooks (this example is for cloning `fieldmapper, or for pulling the latest commits into an already existing clone of `deeplearner`):

# Clone github repository setup
# import join used to join ROOT path and mydrive_path
import os
from os.path import join  

# variables
git_username = "agroimpacts"  # GitHub user/organization name
repo = "fieldmapper"
root = "/content/gdrive/MyDrive/" # set root directory

# save your GitHub access token into a file called "gh.txt", place it in a 
# folder of your choosing. Here we use data/tokens, but change as needed
token_path = f"{root}data/tokens/gh.txt" 
git_token = open(token_path, "r+").read().splitlines()[0]
branch_name = "dev/mc_dropout"

# main path to clone the repo into 
clone_path = f"{root}myprojects"
git_path = f'https://{git_token}@github.com/{git_username}/{repo}.git'
repo_clone_path = f"{clone_path}/{repo}"

# make directory
if not os.path.isdir(clone_path):
    os.makedirs(clone_path)

os.chdir(clone_path)
if not os.path.isdir(repo_clone_path):
    !git clone -b "{branch_name}" "{git_path}"
else:
    if os.listdir(repo_clone_path):
        os.chdir(repo_clone_path)
        !git branch
        !git config core.fileMode false  # needed to ignore permissions changes
        !git pull

os.chdir("..")

That will give you access to fieldmapper, and then you can import it as follows:

import sys, importlib
sys.path.insert(0, os.path.join(repo_clone_path, 'fieldmapper/'))
sys.path.insert(0, repo_clone_path)
import fieldmapper

# uncomment the line below if you make changes to a module during a 
# a session and want to import those changes
# importlib.reload(fieldmapper) 
from fieldmapper.models import *
from fieldmapper.losses import *
from fieldmapper.datatorch import *
from fieldmapper.utils import *
from fieldmapper.compiler import *

The above imports various modules from fieldmapper. You can adapt this approach for your own repo.
The first part of the contents of __init__.py in fieldmapper look like this:
from .datatorch import *
from .utils import *
from .utils_aws import *
from .compiler import *
from .models import *
from .tools import *
from .losses import *
from .metrics import BinaryMetrics
A simpler version of that file is in the maputil folder of the maputil repo:
from .planet_downloader import *
from .rasterize_labels import *
You can follow versions of the above to load modules from your own repo. We will award extra points for taking this more structured approach to developing your project repo.


Exceptions

We realize that time is short and some projects are more experimental than others. For example, we know that difficulties might prevent some projects from getting prediction outputs, or even a fully trained model. We will factor that into assessment.



Assessment
The final project will be assessed out of 70 points. 20 of the points are already allocated to the description (this is basically automatic if it conforms to what is asked). For the remaining 50 points, each sub-team/contributor will be assessed separately for their individual notebooks. We will assess effort based on a combination of git commit histories, as well as documentation of effort in the form of initials added to sections within notebooks or other repo files (e.g. .py).
Points will be assigned as follows:

Quality of notebook (20 points). Does the team/sub-team notebook conform to the specifications set out above, and is the writing, code, and figures clear?

An extra 2.5 points will be awarded to teams that import their main code into analytical steps, rather than rely on all code compiled in notebook cells.

Quality of results (20 points): Did the team demonstrate good progress, sound results, and analysis. I.e. did they get their inputs formatted correctly, ingested into the model, train and evaluate a model, and demonstrate a prediction?

As mentioned above, the ability to achieve all these ingredients will vary between groups and teams, so we will factor those differences into our assessments under this category.
If a group can’t get all the way though model training and prediction, we will evaluate the degree of team progress given project difficulty. Did the team do the best job they could to get as far as they could? Did they try several approaches to overcome problems? Did they adequately document bottlenecks and difficulties? Did they wrap up the project at a point from which further efforts could be readily taken up after submission?

Quality of discussion (10 points): This will assess the quality of insights provided by the team into their results. Does the teams assessment of results against expectations demonstrate understanding of the model, workflow, and analysis. Does the discussion explain likely reasons for bottlenecks/difficulties/unusual or unexpected findings?

Attendance is mandatory. If you need to miss a class, please arrange with one of the instructors in advance. There will be frequent quizzes related to concepts in the assigned reading. These will count towards participation grades.
Another part of attendance is being present when in class. Present means you are paying attention to instructors and not looking at your phone or laptop. title: Course Policies
text:
Technology

In class
The in-person parts of the course are divided into lecture and lab. Lectures will be tech free, pen/pencil and paper note-taking, no phone or laptops (exceptions are of course allowed for accommodations), except for the 2-3 (maybe 4) weeks, when we start doing final projects.
We know this policy might seem odd given that this is a class organized around computation, but there is a fair bit of conceptual material to learn, which in many ways is the most important content, particularly as coding is increasingly handled by agents (see next section). My experience teaching this course to date is that laptops and phones prove to be too much of a distraction (for some, not all), and the conceptual parts are not well absorbed. The conceptual parts are what help you know whether the model or approach you are choosing is appropriate for the task to which you want to apply it.
There are other reasons to adopt a tech-free lecture policy, which are summarized in this New York Times opinion piece from last November. Here are some key passages:

It seems ridiculous to have to say this, but digital distraction is terrible for academic performance. The more time college students spent doing something else on their laptops during class, the lower their exam scores, even after accounting for academic ability.

And regarding notes:

Across 24 studies, college students who took handwritten notes were 58 percent more likely to get A’s in their courses than those who typed notes on laptops. In contrast, students who typed notes were 75 percent more likely to fail the course than those who wrote them by hand.

Lab will be hands-on coding, and will require your laptops.


Use of Artificial Intelligence (AI)
This is a class devoted to learning about the models that underpin AI, and AI-assisted coding is increasingly used by model developers and practitioners as an integral part of their workflow. We will allow and even encourage the use of AI assistants in developing assignments and even your final project. However, we expect the following from you: 1) you show how you used AI as your, which includes documentation of all prompts and responses; 2) that you understand the code you are writing, and do not completely outsource the code yourself. You can code up a complete machine learning pipeline, including a working neural network, quite quickly and run it, but you should understand the model and why it behaves the way it does, which means you have to understand your code. Coding knowledge will be demonstrated by your ability to arrive at correct solutions in your assignments (code completely outsourced to AI will often, if not usually, fail, depending on complexity), and through your grades on a pen and paper coding quiz that we will give. We also reserve the right to give impromptu coding quizzes.
For any writing that you do, e.g. answering quiz and exam questions, writing introductions, methods sections, results, discussions, or other parts of final projects or assignments, AI use is not permitted. Please note that it is very easy for us to tell when it is and isn’t used for writing.
